The right-hand basin has a higher free energy, so the reported product-minus-reactant difference is positive. This difference integrates each basin's probability, including its width:

ΔG(product − reactant) = −RT ln(Pproduct / Preactant)

It is not the difference between the two minimum energies. At fixed volume, this quantity is a Helmholtz free-energy difference, ΔF. The analysis does not add standard-state, concentration, or radial Jacobian corrections.

Provide both reactant=(low, high) and product=(low, high), or neither. Ranges must increase, be disjoint, lie inside the profile, and contain sampled probability. Without them, the implementation tries to infer two geometric basins separated by a fully sampled barrier at least RT above both minima. Check summary["basin_assignment"] and review inferred ranges against the chemistry.

A projected barrier is the intervening profile maximum minus a basin minimum. Its location appears as a dashed line. eyring_proxy_forward and eyring_proxy_reverse, when available, apply the Eyring expression to those projected barriers using kappa (default 1; allowed range 0 < kappa <= 1). They are proxies, not dynamically recovered rates. A one-dimensional projection can hide important coordinates.

docs.title: Reweight a normalized COLVAR
docs.text:
For a metadynamics trajectory, the log weight is:

log(w) = [V(s,t) − c(t) + other biases being removed] / (RT)

PLUMED's metad.rbias contains V − c(t). Alternatively, supply both metad.bias and metad.rct; the analysis subtracts the latter. Raw metadynamics bias alone is insufficient for population reweighting. Do not supply rbias_column and rct_column together.

This small example assigns weights 1, 2, 4, and 8 to four equally populated bins. The most heavily weighted bin becomes the free-energy minimum. Both supported ways of specifying normalization give the same result.

import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

rt = 0.00831446261815324 * 300
q = np.tile([0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5], 10)
rbias = np.tile(rt * np.log([1, 2, 4, 8]), 10)
rct = np.full(len(q), 20.0)
rows = np.column_stack((np.arange(len(q)), q, rbias, rbias + rct, rct))
np.savetxt("weighted-COLVAR", rows,
           header="#! FIELDS time q metad.rbias metad.bias metad.rct", comments="")

common = dict(colvar="weighted-COLVAR", cv="q", cv_unit="dimensionless",
              temperature=300, bins=4, grid_range=(0, 4), smooth_window=0)
fes = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    **common, rbias_column="metad.rbias"))
equivalent = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    **common, bias_column="metad.bias", rct_column="metad.rct"))
np.testing.assert_allclose(fes.free_energy, equivalent.free_energy)
print("Relative energies:", np.round(fes.free_energy, 3), "kJ/mol")
print("Weight effective sample size:",
      round(fes.summary["sampling"]["weight_effective_sample_size"], 2))
fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(fes, show_basins=False)
ax.set_title("Known weights: 1, 2, 4, 8")

COLVAR must contain a time column with strictly increasing times and regularly spaced selected samples. start_time and end_time select an inclusive interval in the file's time units. At least two samples must remain. bins is an integer of at least 3; grid_range=(low, high) fixes the histogram edges. Keep this range and the number of bins fixed when comparing profiles.

The parser accepts repeated identical headers. When reading a COLVAR being written by a live simulation, it omits an unfinished final line and records a warning. Completed malformed rows, changing headers, and duplicate or decreasing times are errors. Do not concatenate restarted trajectories without first resolving time resets.

docs.title: Inspect a histogram and its unsampled regions
docs.text:
An unbiased trajectory has unit weights. The same analysis API can represent that case with an explicitly zero bias column. Use zeros only when the samples are actually unbiased; they cannot correct a metadynamics run with missing bias information.

import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

rng = np.random.default_rng(14)
q = np.r_[rng.normal(-0.9, 0.12, 900), rng.normal(0.9, 0.12, 600)]
rng.shuffle(q)
rows = np.column_stack((np.arange(len(q)) * 0.1, q, np.zeros(len(q))))
np.savetxt("unbiased-COLVAR", rows,
           header="#! FIELDS time q unbiased_weight", comments="")

fes = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    colvar="unbiased-COLVAR", cv="q", temperature=300,
    rbias_column="unbiased_weight", bins=60, grid_range=(-1.5, 1.5),
    reactant=(-1.5, -0.3), product=(0.3, 1.5), smooth_window=0,
))
for name, value in fes.summary["sampling"].items():
    print(name, ":", value)
print("Finite bins:", np.isfinite(fes.free_energy).sum())
print("Forward barrier available:", "eyring_proxy_forward" in fes.summary)
fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(fes)
ax.set_title("An unsampled gap stays a gap")

Empty histogram bins have +inf free energy and appear as gaps. The library neither adds pseudocounts nor interpolates a barrier across these bins. Basin populations can still be reported, but a missing path between their minima prevents a resolved barrier and Eyring proxy.

Read fes.summary["sampling"] before interpreting a COLVAR profile:

Diagnostic Interpretation samples, start_time, end_time Number and time range of selected observations empty_bins Bins with no selected observations samples_outside_grid Selected samples excluded by the histogram range weight_effective_sample_size (sum w)^2 / sum(w^2); a small value means a few weighted frames dominate

The effective sample size is a weight diagnostic over selected frames, including frames outside the grid. It does not correct for temporal correlation and is not an uncertainty estimate. Inspect fes.warnings, input field ranges in summary["inputs"], and any barrier_unavailable or profile_unavailable explanation as well.

docs.title: Read defaults and walls from the saved PLUMED input
docs.text:
plumed_input="plumed.dat" can infer the CV, temperature, units, PRINT output path, bias labels, and supported wall definitions. Relative input paths are resolved against the saved PLUMED file. Explicit analysis settings override inferred defaults. Input parsing supports the common single-line and ACTION ... block syntax, with exactly one METAD action on one explicit CV; it is not a general PLUMED preprocessor.

This example writes a small saved input and a matching synthetic COLVAR. Its recorded wall energy is removed automatically in the default analysis. keep_wall=True retains that restraint, so the two curves answer different thermodynamic questions.

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

Path("wall-example.dat").write_text(
    "UNITS LENGTH=nm ENERGY=kj/mol TIME=ps\n"
    "q: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2\n"
    "metad: METAD ARG=q SIGMA=0.02 HEIGHT=1 PACE=100 BIASFACTOR=10 TEMP=300\n"
    "wall: UPPER_WALLS ARG=q AT=0.8 KAPPA=100 EXP=2\n"
    "PRINT ARG=q,metad.rbias,wall.bias FILE=wall-COLVAR STRIDE=10\n"
)
q = np.tile(np.linspace(0.1, 1.1, 11), 20)
wall = 100 * np.maximum(q - 0.8, 0)**2
np.savetxt("wall-COLVAR", np.column_stack((np.arange(len(q)), q, q * 0, wall)),
           header="#! FIELDS time q metad.rbias wall.bias", comments="")

common = dict(plumed_input="wall-example.dat", bins=11,
              grid_range=(0.05, 1.15), smooth_window=0)
removed = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(**common))
retained = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(**common, keep_wall=True))
fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(removed, show_basins=False, label="Wall removed")
Plot().fes_1d(retained, ax=ax, show_basins=False,
              label="Wall retained", color="#d48122")
print("Inferred units:", removed.cv_unit, removed.summary["input_energy_unit"])

Without saved input, set additional_bias=("wall.bias",) to add that recorded bias to the population log weights. You are choosing which restraints to remove; the code cannot infer the desired physical ensemble from a column name alone.

For an existing FES or a HILLS reconstruction, upper_wall=(at, kappa) subtracts the quadratic energy kappa * max(q − at, 0)^2 in the input energy units. With hills and plumed_input, a compatible single-CV quadratic upper wall can be inferred automatically, including its EPS/OFFSET settings. keep_wall=True disables inferred wall removal. Do not combine it with upper_wall. Lower or more complex walls require an appropriate explicit treatment. Removing a wall's energy cannot recover a region the trajectory never sampled.

docs.title: Reconstruct from HILLS on your computer
docs.text:
Use this local workflow when a run has HILLS but lacks normalized COLVAR weights:

from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

simulation = mlmd()
fes = simulation.analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    hills="run/HILLS", plumed_input="run/plumed.dat",
    bins=200, grid_range=(0.15, 0.8),
    # plumed="/path/to/plumed",  # optional explicit executable
    output_dir="hills-analysis", plot=True,
))
fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(fes, energy_unit="kcal/mol")

The executable is found beside the current Python executable or on PATH, unless plumed is supplied. This calls plumed sum_hills and reads its output. PLUMED already applies the well-tempered scaling: do not multiply the returned energies by the bias-factor correction again. If no grid_range is given, the range is inferred from the deposited hill centers. Inspect that choice rather than assuming it includes every region of interest.

Choose hills or fes_file, not both. grid_range and bins configure reconstruction or histogramming; they do not resample an existing FES file. grid_range is rejected with fes_file. Time-window selection and population-reweighting column arguments apply to COLVAR, not HILLS or supplied FES grids.

For older COLVAR files containing only raw bias, plumed_input plus the matching HILLS and explicit METAD grid bounds can recover missing c(t) using PLUMED. This recovery supports a nonperiodic, one-dimensional, single-walker, fixed-width well-tempered run with a constant bias factor greater than one. The grid must cover all samples and hill centers. Reconstructed and recorded raw bias must agree within 0.01 kJ/mol; inconsistent histories are rejected. Read summary["bias_reconstruction"] and its warnings. This path also requires local PLUMED.

docs.title: Periodic CVs and multidimensional profiles
docs.text:
Simulation setup can define a torsion CV, but this analysis currently has no periodic-boundary-crossing basin or barrier treatment. FES grids marked periodic are rejected. COLVAR histogramming treats its numeric coordinate as a line; it does not join -pi to pi. A basin split across that seam will therefore be misrepresented unless you first choose and validate a suitable unwrapped reaction path. Simply deleting periodic metadata does not make the analysis valid.

Multidimensional HILLS and repeated-coordinate FES tables are also unsupported. Prepare a physically appropriate one-dimensional marginal grid externally before using fes_file; do not flatten a multidimensional surface into a one-dimensional list. These restrictions are distinct from periodic simulation cells: a nonperiodic distance CV measured in a periodic cell can still be suitable for this analysis.

docs.title: Compare time blocks before interpreting the profile
docs.text:
One profile does not establish convergence, and the API does not automatically calculate block uncertainties. Compare time windows on the same grid, inspect repeated transitions, and check stability against bin resolution and independent runs. The following creates three independent synthetic blocks with the same underlying distribution, then compares their basin free energies.

import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

rng = np.random.default_rng(27)
centers = np.linspace(-1.45, 1.45, 30)
target_energy = 6 * (centers**2 - 1)**2 + 0.5 * centers
probability = np.exp(-target_energy / (0.00831446261815324 * 300))
probability /= probability.sum()
block_size = 2000
q = rng.choice(centers, size=3 * block_size, p=probability)
np.savetxt("blocks-COLVAR", np.column_stack((np.arange(len(q)), q, q * 0)),
           header="#! FIELDS time q unbiased_weight", comments="")

differences = []
ax = None
for block, color in enumerate(("#235789", "#d48122", "#38995b")):
    fes = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
        colvar="blocks-COLVAR", cv="q", temperature=300,
        rbias_column="unbiased_weight", bins=30, grid_range=(-1.5, 1.5),
        start_time=block * block_size, end_time=(block + 1) * block_size - 1,
        reactant=(-1.5, -0.4), product=(0.4, 1.5), smooth_window=0,
    ))
    differences.append(fes.summary["delta_g_product_minus_reactant_kj_mol"])
    fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(fes, ax=ax, show_basins=False,
                          label=f"Block {block + 1}", color=color)
print("Block basin differences:", np.round(differences, 3), "kJ/mol")
print("Sample standard deviation:", round(float(np.std(differences, ddof=1)), 3))
ax.set_title("Compare profiles with identical histogram edges")

The displayed standard deviation describes these three block estimates. It is not automatically a confidence interval or a standard error for a correlated molecular trajectory. Real blocks must be long enough to address correlation and explore the relevant states; biased trajectories also need valid weights in each selected interval. Agreement among undersampled windows can be misleading.

Analyze separate equilibrium runs separately. A list of COLVAR files is reserved for independent infrequent first-passage runs with infrequent=True; it is not an equilibrium-pooling option.

docs.title: Smooth the display and export results
docs.text:
smooth_window defaults to 11 points. Set it to 0 to disable smoothing, or to an odd integer of at least 5. The implementation fits a local cubic polynomial, not a Gaussian kernel. It smooths each finite sampled segment independently, reduces the window for short segments, and leaves segments shorter than five points unchanged. Gaps remain gaps. The smoothed curve is shifted to a zero minimum.

Smoothing affects the plotted curve and optional smoothed CSV. Basin populations, barriers, and rate estimates use the raw profile. A smooth curve is not evidence of convergence. There is no Gaussian-smoothing configuration option.

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd, Plot

q = np.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 101)
energy_kcal = (8 * (q**2 - 1)**2 + 0.4 * np.sin(35 * q)) / 4.184
np.savetxt("noisy-fes.dat", np.column_stack((q, energy_kcal)),
           header="#! FIELDS q energy", comments="")

simulation = mlmd()
directory = simulation.analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    fes_file="noisy-fes.dat", cv="q", temperature=300,
    energy_column="energy", energy_unit="kcal/mol", cv_unit="dimensionless",
    smooth_window=11, output_dir="analysis-export", plot=True, overwrite=True,
), output_format="files")
fes = simulation.data
print("Saved:", ", ".join(path.name for path in sorted(directory.iterdir())))
print("Stored energy units:", fes.energy_unit)
fig, ax = Plot().fes_1d(fes, energy_unit="kcal/mol", show_raw=True,
                       show_basins=False, label="Local cubic smoothing")
ax.set_title("Input, display, and export units are explicit")

The generated CSV, JSON, and PNG files appear as downloads under the browser example. In a local run they are written into output_dir. Set overwrite=True only when replacing earlier analysis outputs is intended; it is enabled here to make repeated clicks work. Input files are protected from being overwritten by output filenames.

Output Contents free_energy.csv Coordinate and raw relative free energy in kJ/mol free_energy_smoothed.csv Display-smoothed profile, only when smoothing is enabled summary.json Source files, method, units, diagnostics, basin results, and warnings free_energy.png Plot when plot=True and a profile is available

The default output_format="data" returns the Data object. It still writes files when output_dir is supplied. output_format="files" requires output_dir and returns a Path; the Data object remains available as simulation.data. plot=True also requires an output directory.

The returned object's main attributes are x, free_energy, free_energy_smoothed, two-column data, energy_unit, cv, cv_unit, temperature_K, summary, and warnings. Plot.fes_1d() returns (figure, axes) and retains them as plot.fig and plot.ax. Use energy_unit to change display units, smooth_window to override display smoothing, show_raw to show the original curve under a smoothed one, and show_basins to control basin shading and the barrier marker. ax, color, and label support overlays as shown above. Display changes do not alter the stored raw energy array.

docs.title: Analyze independent infrequent-metadynamics passages
docs.text:
First-passage analysis has a different data contract from equilibrium population reweighting. It needs independent runs starting at time zero in the explicit reactant range, with strictly increasing times. Each run ends at its first recorded entry into the product range, or contributes right-censored exposure if no entry is observed.

Use the cumulative PLUMED acceleration column when available (acceleration_column="metad.acc"), or the raw nonnegative bias (bias_column="metad.bias"). A normalized rbias is not a kinetic acceleration bias. The estimator is events divided by total accelerated exposure. With no events, the result is a one-sided exponential rate bound instead of a measured zero rate.

import numpy as np
from matmalib import mlmd

rt = 0.00831446261815324 * 300
paths = []
for label, endpoint in (("event", 0.30), ("censored", 0.22)):
    path = f"passage-{label}.COLVAR"
    rows = np.column_stack(([0, 1, 2], [0.20, 0.23, endpoint],
                            np.full(3, rt * np.log(10))))
    np.savetxt(path, rows, header="#! FIELDS time q metad.bias", comments="")
    paths.append(path)

result = mlmd().analyze_metadynamics(mlmd.AnalysisConfig(
    colvar=paths, cv="q", cv_unit="nm", temperature=300, time_unit="ps",
    infrequent=True, bias_column="metad.bias",
    reactant=(0.18, 0.25), product=(0.28, 0.35),
))
for name in ("independent_runs", "events", "right_censored_runs", "rate_s_inv"):
    print(name, ":", result.summary[name])
print("FES available:", len(result.x) > 0)
print(result.summary["profile_unavailable"])

The constant synthetic bias gives an acceleration factor of 10: each two-picosecond record contributes 20 ps of accelerated exposure. One event over 40 ps gives 2.5e10 s⁻¹. This arithmetic example does not validate the physical assumptions of infrequent metadynamics.

The method assumes sufficiently infrequent deposition, negligible transition-state bias, independent equilibrated reactant starts, and exponential escape statistics. Active additional restraint-bias columns before first passage are rejected; adding a wall's energy to an acceleration factor is not a general kinetic correction. Output stride limits the event time resolution. Raw-bias integration should be checked against finer output; a recorded cumulative acceleration is preferable when available.

At least five uncensored independent runs enable a reproducible parametric-bootstrap exponential-fit diagnostic in the summary. Its p-value is a fit diagnostic, not proof of unbiased kinetics. kappa enters the reported activation-free-energy conversion and Eyring proxies, not the event/exposure rate estimator.

A kinetics-only result can have empty x and free_energy arrays. Do not pass it to Plot.fes_1d(). You can supply a suitable hills or fes_file alongside the independent COLVAR runs to analyze a profile as well. summary.json is still exportable when no FES is available.

Continue with the MLMD API and configuration reference and the script feature map. For the existing two-coordinate count-based landscape, see free-energy and population maps; Plot.fes() does not perform this metadynamics reweighting.

docs.title: Run metadynamics with PLUMED
docs.text:
mlmd.run_md can add a PLUMED bias to an ASE-compatible potential. The built-in configuration generates well-tempered metadynamics for one distance, angle, or torsion; custom PLUMED input supports additional actions and multiple collective variables (CVs). This tutorial covers configuration, native execution, outputs, continuous equilibration, and restart.

Metadynamics deposits history-dependent hills along selected CVs. Choosing a CV, Gaussian width, deposition interval, and bias strength requires physical knowledge of the process being sampled; faster motion in a chosen CV alone does not establish a converged free-energy surface. See the PLUMED METAD documentation for the method and action options.

docs.title: 1. Install native PLUMED
docs.text:
Use the repository's environment from its root directory:

conda env update -n matmalib -f environment.yml
conda run -n matmalib python -m pip check
conda activate matmalib

It installs the MLMD dependencies plus the native PLUMED kernel, Python bindings, command-line tools, and FFTW. pip install 'matmalib[metadynamics]' supplies ASE and Python bindings for a supplied calculator, but the bindings alone do not include the native kernel. For AIMNet, use the full MLMD setup in the simulation tutorial.

Browser cells on this page only create configurations and inspect units. Running a simulation needs the local environment; PLUMED and AIMNet are not loaded in the browser.

docs.title: 2. Understand indices, units, and timing
docs.text:
The two interfaces intentionally use different conventions:

Quantity MD/geometry interface Generated PLUMED input Atom selections fixed_atoms uses zero-based positions MetadynamicsConfig.atoms uses one-based positions Length Å nm Energy eV kJ/mol Time fs ps in HILLS/COLVAR Angles Geometry methods commonly return degrees ANGLE, TORSION, and their sigma use radians Temperature K K Frequency Integration steps pace and colvar_stride are integration-step counts

PLUMED's default units apply to input parameters and output files; custom input can change them with an initial UNITS directive. See PLUMED UNITS.

from matmalib import mlmd

meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(atoms=(3, 11), sigma=0.02, pace=300,
                               colvar_stride=10)
md = mlmd.MDConfig(steps=100000, timestep_fs=0.5,
                   mode="metadynamics", metadynamics=meta)
print("Selected zero-based positions:", tuple(i - 1 for i in meta.atoms))
print("Distance width:", 10 * meta.sigma, "angstrom")
print("Hill interval:", meta.pace * md.timestep_fs, "fs")
print("COLVAR interval:", meta.colvar_stride * md.timestep_fs / 1000, "ps")
print("Run duration:", md.steps * md.timestep_fs / 1000, "ps")

The example reports a 0.2 Å width, 150 fs hill interval, 0.005 ps COLVAR interval, and 50 ps duration. These are illustrative settings, not a validated protocol for a particular molecule. Changing the timestep changes every frequency expressed in physical time unless you adjust the corresponding step counts.

Use positions in the input atom ordering, not Atom.id, PDB serial numbers, or residue identifiers. Atom selections must contain the required number of unique, valid one-based indices.

docs.title: 3. Run a small installation check
docs.text:
Save the following as check_metadynamics.py and run python check_metadynamics.py in a new directory. This exercises native PLUMED with ASE's inexpensive EMT calculator and a small copper cell. It is an integration check, not a machine-learning model or a physical free-energy calculation. It avoids downloading model weights.

from pathlib import Path
from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

out = Path("metad_check")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())
meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(
    cv="DISTANCE", atoms=(1, 2),
    sigma=0.02, height_kj_mol=0.1, pace=10,
    biasfactor=10.0, colvar_stride=1,
    calc_rct=True, grid_auto=True,
    hills_file=out / "HILLS",
    colvar_file=out / "COLVAR",
    save_input=out / "plumed.dat",
    log_file=out / "plumed.log",
)
trajectory = simulation.run_md(
    bulk("Cu", cubic=True),
    mlmd.MDConfig(
        steps=100, timestep_fs=0.2, temperature_K=300.0,
        ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin", seed=17,
        mode="metadynamics", metadynamics=meta,
        trajectory=out / "trajectory.xyz",
        trajectory_interval=10,
        log_file=out / "md.log",
        log_interval=10,
    ),
)
print("Trajectory:", trajectory)
print("Checkpoint:", simulation.data.checkpoint_file)
print("Final step:", simulation.data.last_step)
print("Resolved PLUMED:")
print("\n".join(simulation.data.plumed_input))

Expect a streamed XYZ trajectory through step 100, an MD log, a final checkpoint, and PLUMED input/log/HILLS/COLVAR files. The simulation lasts only 20 fs. Re-running with the same names raises instead of silently replacing files; select a new output directory for another check.

For a molecular MLMD calculation, use simulation = mlmd(...) with appropriate AIMNet weights or another validated ASE calculator, and replace the copper structure with your equilibrated State or extended XYZ path. Choose the CV atoms for that system. The solvation tutorial creates equilibrated.xyz; retain its cell and PBC metadata for a periodic run.

docs.title: 4. Choose a generated CV and bias
docs.text:
Setting Meaning cv="DISTANCE", atoms=(i, j) One scalar separation; sigma and wall positions in nm. cv="ANGLE", atoms=(i, j, k) Angle at the middle atom; width and wall positions in radians. cv="TORSION", atoms=(i, j, k, l) Signed dihedral using the supplied ordering; width and wall positions in radians. height_kj_mol Positive initial hill height. pace Positive integer number of integration steps between hills. biasfactor Well-tempered factor, strictly greater than one. temperature_K Bias temperature; None uses the enclosing MD temperature. cv_label, metad_label, wall_label Distinct PLUMED action labels; defaults cv, metad, wall. metad_arg, wall_arg Default to the CV label; references must correspond to available actions. colvar_stride, colvar_arg PRINT frequency and optional comma-separated output references.

For nonperiodic systems, generated CV input includes NOPBC. For periodic systems PLUMED uses the box supplied at each step. Partial periodicity is rejected: use either no periodic axes or full three-dimensional PBC. If your CV needs molecule reconstruction or a special treatment of periodic images, express it in custom PLUMED input rather than assuming wrapped coordinates are sufficient.

The generated form defines one scalar CV. Use custom input for a multidimensional bias, combinations of CVs, or other PLUMED actions. metad_arg changes references; it does not create additional CV definitions.

docs.title: Add an optional wall
docs.text:
from matmalib import mlmd

meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(
    cv="DISTANCE", atoms=(1, 2),
    wall_type="UPPER_WALLS",
    wall_at=0.6, wall_kappa=150000.0,
    wall_exp=2, wall_eps=1.0, wall_offset=0.0,
)
print("Wall location:", meta.wall_at * 10, "angstrom")
print("Wall action:", meta.wall_type)
print("Energy scale:", meta.wall_kappa, "in generated PLUMED energy units")

UPPER_WALLS or LOWER_WALLS enables a wall; wall_type=None disables it. wall_at/wall_offset follow the CV units. wall_kappa, wall_exp, and wall_eps control the PLUMED wall potential. A strong wall can produce large forces and restrict accessible states; choose its location and stiffness deliberately. The resulting wall.bias is printed by default and matters when interpreting or removing bias in analysis.

docs.title: Decide whether to use a grid and normalized bias
docs.text:
calc_rct=True requests PLUMED's normalization estimate and adds metad.rbias and metad.rct to the default COLVAR columns. It requires a bias grid. Those columns enable normalized population reweighting in the analysis tutorial; raw metad.bias alone is not used as a normalized population weight.

Situation Configuration Fully periodic, fixed-cell scalar DISTANCE Defaults grid_auto=None, calc_rct=None select an automatic grid and normalized bias when no explicit grid is supplied. Same system, explicit bounds Set grid_min, grid_max, grid_bins, and grid_auto=False; use calc_rct=True for normalized bias. Nonperiodic distance, angle, or torsion No automatic grid. Supply an appropriate complete grid for normalized bias, or use calc_rct=False. NPT distance Automatic bounds are disabled because the cell evolves. Use explicit bounds with grid_auto=False, or disable normalization and analyze HILLS.

Automatic distance bounds are derived from the fixed cell's half-cell corners, converted to nm, and extended by a margin related to sigma. grid_spacing defaults to 0.002 nm and controls the resulting bin count. Automatic grid_min must be finite and at most zero. For explicit grids, both grid_max and a positive integer grid_bins are required, with grid_min < grid_max; setting calc_rct=True without a complete grid raises.

For example, an explicit distance grid could be configured as follows after choosing bounds that contain your sampled distances and hill support:

meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(
    atoms=(3, 11), sigma=0.02,
    grid_auto=False, grid_min=0.0, grid_max=3.0, grid_bins=1500,
    calc_rct=True,
    hills_file="npt_HILLS", colvar_file="npt_COLVAR",
    save_input="npt_plumed.dat",
)

The 3 nm bound is an example, not an automatic guarantee for an expanding NPT cell. For a torsion, use a domain consistent with its angular periodicity and the native PLUMED action; do not reuse a distance grid. Matmalib's FES analysis is currently one-dimensional and does not support a basin crossing a periodic boundary.

NPT additionally requires full PBC, a finite-volume cell, a stress-capable potential, and no fixed-atom, SHAKE, or center-of-mass constraints. The PLUMED virial contributes to pressure/stress, and the bias is updated once per integration step even if the integrator requests several force evaluations. A time-dependent bias also means that choosing ensemble="NVE" does not yield conservation of the unbiased system's energy.

docs.title: 5. Supply custom PLUMED input
docs.text:
Use either plumed_file or input_lines. These replace generated CV/bias/wall/PRINT commands; fields such as atoms, sigma, hills_file, and colvar_file no longer define the custom actions or their destinations.

This configuration defines two distances and a two-dimensional bias. It assumes at least four atoms; pair choices and hill widths must suit your system:

from pathlib import Path
from matmalib import mlmd

out = Path("custom_bias").resolve()
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(
    input_lines=(
        "UNITS LENGTH=nm ENERGY=kj/mol TIME=ps",
        "d1: DISTANCE ATOMS=1,2",
        "d2: DISTANCE ATOMS=3,4",
        f"m: METAD ARG=d1,d2 SIGMA=0.02,0.02 HEIGHT=1 PACE=300 "
        f"BIASFACTOR=10 TEMP=300 FILE={out / 'HILLS'}",
        f"PRINT ARG=d1,d2,m.bias STRIDE=10 FILE={out / 'COLVAR'}",
    ),
    save_input=out / "plumed.dat",
    log_file=out / "plumed.log",
)
# In your prepared workflow:
# simulation.run_md(ready, mlmd.MDConfig(
#     mode="metadynamics", metadynamics=meta,
#     trajectory=out / "trajectory.xyz", log_file=out / "md.log",
# ))

Alternatively, mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(plumed_file="my_plumed.dat", save_input="resolved.dat") reads an existing file. Comments and blank lines are stripped, and PLUMED ... blocks are flattened; nested or unterminated blocks are rejected. save_input stores that resolved input, also available as simulation.data.plumed_input.

Custom commands control their own paths, units, periodic treatment, and restart directives. Relative output paths are interpreted by the native run, not automatically relative to plumed_file; use explicit paths for reproducibility. Matmalib's generated-output path protections do not inspect every custom FILE action, so use a fresh directory and avoid accidental reuse. The one-dimensional analysis API cannot directly reconstruct this two-dimensional example; use PLUMED tools or a separately prepared one-dimensional marginal grid.

docs.title: 6. Keep a live bias through equilibration
docs.text:
Ordinary preparation is unbiased unless its own configuration explicitly requests metadynamics. To build the bias during equilibration and continue it during production, use one shared MetadynamicsConfig and continue_equilibration_bias=True in a single run_md call:

from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd()
meta = mlmd.MetadynamicsConfig(
    atoms=(3, 11),
    hills_file="continuous_HILLS", colvar_file="continuous_COLVAR",
    save_input="continuous_plumed.dat", log_file="continuous_plumed.log",
)
equilibration = mlmd.EquilibrationConfig(
    steps=2000, timestep_fs=0.5, temperature_K=300,
    ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin", thermostat_time_fs=10,
    mode="metadynamics", metadynamics=meta,
    trajectory="biased_equilibration.xyz", log_file="biased_equilibration.log",
    seed=31,
)
simulation.run_md("equilibrated.xyz", mlmd.MDConfig(
    steps=100000, timestep_fs=0.5, temperature_K=300,
    ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin", thermostat_time_fs=100,
    mode="metadynamics", metadynamics=meta,
    equilibration=equilibration, continue_equilibration_bias=True,
    trajectory="biased_production.xyz", log_file="biased_production.log",
    seed=31,
))
print(simulation.data.start_step, simulation.data.last_step)  # 2000, 102000

The live PLUMED instance, hill history, velocities, RNG, and clock continue across the boundary. HILLS/COLVAR remain shared; MD trajectories and logs have separate paths. Thermostat damping may change. Both phases must use identical timestep, target temperature, ensemble, metadynamics settings, and potential; cell/PBC/charge/multiplicity overrides must agree. Seeds must match when both are set. NPT retains the cell reached during equilibration.

This also supports custom PLUMED input while the process remains alive. It is different from ending equilibrate and then starting an independent run_md: returning a State preserves molecular state but does not preserve a live PLUMED bias. Independent biased phases should use separate bias files unless you implement an explicit native restart workflow.

docs.title: 7. Restart generated metadynamics safely
docs.text:
By default, checkpoints are written every 1,000 steps and at completion, including biased runs. checkpoint_interval changes the interval and checkpoint_file=None disables them. Save simulation.data.checkpoint_file before performing another operation that replaces .data.

After the installation check above, run:

from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())  # same potential as the original check
continued = simulation.restart_md(
    "metad_check/trajectory.checkpoint.npz",
    steps=50,
    trajectory="metad_check/part2.xyz",
    log_file="metad_check/part2.log",
)
print(continued)
print(simulation.data.last_step)  # 150

steps means additional integration steps. Restart restores molecular state, constraints, random-generator state, thermostat/barostat variables, and the original step count. Use the same ASE version and model/calculator settings; model weights are not embedded in a checkpoint.

The new XYZ/log files are separate segments; existing files are protected. For generated PLUMED input, saved HILLS/COLVAR snapshots are copied to part2.plumed/, the saved input is updated to those paths, and native restart continues the bias and output history there. Original files are untouched. HILLS text precision can produce small numerical differences from an uninterrupted biased run.

overwrite=True is permission to replace output paths during a new run; it is not a continuation or append switch. Use restart_md for checkpoint continuation or continue_equilibration_bias for live phase continuation. Custom PLUMED runs still write molecular-state checkpoints, but restart_md rejects them because arbitrary actions may need additional state beyond HILLS/COLVAR. Handle custom native restart requirements explicitly rather than treating their checkpoint as a complete automatic bias restart.

docs.title: 8. Inspect the result before analysis
docs.text:
Output Contents Extended XYZ trajectory Saved geometry, cell/PBC, masses, momenta, step, and time_fs; streamed to disk. MD log Potential/kinetic/total energy, temperature, maximum force, volume, and timing; unavailable model-disagreement fields are nan. HILLS Deposited-hill history, used by native bias restart and reconstruction. COLVAR CV and available bias columns at colvar_stride; generated times are in ps. Saved PLUMED input Resolved action definitions and paths for provenance and analysis. simulation.data Status, bounded running statistics, model/system/settings metadata, resolved input, and checkpoint paths.

In biased runs, potential and total energies in MD diagnostics include the applied bias; they are not an unbiased energy-conservation trace. Inspect CV coverage, numerical stability, hill history, and sensitivity to discarded equilibration and sampling duration before interpreting a FES. Continue to metadynamics analysis for normalized COLVAR reweighting, HILLS reconstruction, and one-dimensional free-energy plots.

docs.title: Checkpoint and restart an MD simulation
docs.text:
restart_md continues the integrator from a saved snapshot and writes a new trajectory segment. Use it when stopping a long calculation, recovering from an interrupted run, or splitting a calculation across jobs. A geometry file retains atoms and momenta but does not contain all the random-generator, thermostat/barostat, or bias state required for faithful continuation.

This tutorial uses only the md extra and ASE's small EMT calculator. It downloads no ML model and needs no PLUMED installation. For AIMNet runs, construct the restart interface with the same model files, calculator options, and device setup you used originally.

docs.title: 1. Save a checkpoint and continue in another process
docs.text:
From a current source checkout, install the small simulation extra:

python -m pip install -e '.[md]'

Save this as first_segment.py and run python first_segment.py:

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())
simulation.run_md(
    bulk("Cu", cubic=True),
    mlmd.MDConfig(
        steps=12, timestep_fs=0.2, temperature_K=100,
        ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin", seed=31,
        trajectory="restart_run/part1.xyz", trajectory_interval=2,
        log_file="restart_run/part1.log", log_interval=2,
        checkpoint_interval=5,
        checkpoint_file="restart_run/part1.checkpoint.npz",
    ),
)
print("Last step:", simulation.data.last_step)
print("Snapshot step:", simulation.data.checkpoint_step)
print("Checkpoint:", simulation.data.checkpoint_file)

Snapshots are written after steps 5 and 10, then at the final step 12. The same checkpoint path is atomically replaced each time; it is not an archive of all earlier checkpoints. Expect both printed step values to be 12.

Save the next script as second_segment.py and run it in a fresh Python process from the same working directory:

from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())
trajectory = simulation.restart_md(
    "restart_run/part1.checkpoint.npz",
    steps=8,
    trajectory="restart_run/part2.xyz",
    log_file="restart_run/part2.log",
)
report = simulation.data
print("Additional steps:", report.steps)
print("Step range:", report.start_step, report.last_step)
print("Absolute final time (fs):", report.time_fs)
print("Segment duration (fs):", report.simulation_time_fs)
print("New trajectory:", trajectory)
print("New checkpoint:", report.checkpoint_file)
print("Restarted from:", report.restarted_from)

Expect 8 additional steps, step range 12–20, absolute time 4 fs, and segment duration 1.6 fs. Restart keeps the saved timestep, ensemble, temperature, coupling parameters, and output/checkpoint intervals. This API does not accept a replacement MDConfig: a changed protocol is a new run, not an exact continuation.

The new segment includes the checkpoint geometry as its first frame, with step 12 and time 2.4 fs. The original segment also ends at step 12. When combining segments for analysis, discard one copy of that shared boundary frame. Do not blindly generate a new time axis starting at zero for each segment.

docs.title: 2. Understand the saved state
docs.text:
Checkpoints use a ZIP-based .npz container with JSON metadata and NumPy arrays, without pickle. They include:

Saved information Why it matters Atomic numbers, coordinates, cell, and PBC The current molecular geometry and periodic box. Masses, momenta, and velocities Preserve mass scaling and the instantaneous dynamical state. Charge, multiplicity, and constraints Preserve the system specification, including initialized SHAKE target lengths. Configuration and step/time counters Continue the same protocol and label output continuously. NumPy random-generator state Continue Langevin random forces without redrawing the velocity distribution. ASE integrator variables Restore extended thermostat/barostat coordinates and momenta. Generated PLUMED input and bias snapshots, when applicable Reconstruct supported metadynamics history.

Model weights and the calculator object are not embedded. Recreate the same calculator and use the same inference weights and settings. Custom calculators with their own mutable state beyond the saved atomic/integrator state must manage that state separately. The loader requires exactly the ASE version recorded in the checkpoint and rejects incompatible integrator fields or inconsistent arrays. Preserve your environment and model versions alongside a research run; arbitrary cross-version or cross-hardware bitwise identity is not promised.

You can inspect a checkpoint using standard libraries and NumPy without importing the private checkpoint implementation. Run this after the first segment:

import json
from zipfile import ZipFile
import numpy as np

path = "restart_run/part1.checkpoint.npz"
with ZipFile(path) as archive:
    metadata = json.loads(archive.read("metadata.json"))
print("Format/version:", metadata["format"], metadata["version"])
print("ASE version:", metadata["ase_version"])
print("Integrator:", metadata["integrator"])
print("Saved step/time:", metadata["step"], metadata["time_fs"])
with np.load(path, allow_pickle=False) as arrays:
    print("Positions:", arrays["positions"].shape)
    print("Velocities (angstrom/fs):", arrays["velocities_angstrom_fs"].shape)

Treat the snapshot as a restart artifact rather than editing its JSON/arrays. Restart validates and restores constraints and integrator state together; manually changing one field can make the stored state inconsistent.

docs.title: 3. Configure the schedule and file names
docs.text:
from dataclasses import replace
from matmalib import mlmd

config = mlmd.MDConfig(
    steps=2300,
    trajectory="production.xyz",
    checkpoint_interval=1000,
)
# An ordinary new run begins at step zero.
scheduled = list(range(config.checkpoint_interval, config.steps + 1,
                       config.checkpoint_interval))
if not scheduled or scheduled[-1] != config.steps:
    scheduled.append(config.steps)
print("Planned snapshot steps:", scheduled)
print("Checkpoint selection:", config.checkpoint_file)
print("Disable checkpoints:", replace(config, checkpoint_file=None).checkpoint_file)

For a fresh 2,300-step run this plans snapshots at 1,000, 2,000, and 2,300. All MD and equilibration ensembles use the same default schedule of every 1,000 steps and at completion, including unbiased MD and generated or custom PLUMED input. A successful zero-step run also writes a final snapshot. No initial snapshot is written for a nonzero-length run, so a failure before its first scheduled save may leave no checkpoint.

Option Behavior checkpoint_file="auto" Derive the path from the trajectory basename, replacing its suffix with .checkpoint.npz. Equilibration without a trajectory Derive the path from its log basename, or use equilibration.checkpoint.npz if no log is configured. checkpoint_file="my_snapshot.npz" Use an explicit checkpoint path. checkpoint_file=None Disable snapshot writes. checkpoint_interval=N Save at absolute step multiples of positive integer N and at completion.

On restart, the checkpoint interval is inherited; for a snapshot at step 12 with interval 5, the next periodic save is step 15. The restart method's checkpoint_file argument can choose a new destination or disable new snapshots. Its default "auto" uses the new trajectory's basename.

If trajectory is omitted from restart_md, the filename includes the original output basename and saved step, such as part1.restart-12.xyz, beside the checkpoint. log_file=None is the restart default: it disables a new text log rather than appending to the original log. Reports and the new trajectory are still produced.

Restart always protects existing outputs and does not expose an overwrite flag. Use new trajectory/log/checkpoint paths for each continuation. It also rejects a checkpoint destination equal to its input snapshot. The original snapshot remains unchanged, allowing independent branches with different new output names.

docs.title: 4. Know what is resumed and what is skipped
docs.text:
Restart restores velocities instead of thermalizing them, restores the random-generator state, and does not apply hydrogen/heavy-atom mass changes again. The saved configuration removes preparation phases, so minimization and equilibration are not rerun. This is true even when the original production run embedded those phases.

run_md("previous.xyz", config) is useful when deliberately starting a new protocol from its last geometry, but it creates new integrator/RNG state and new step/time labels. Extended XYZ preserves momenta, allowing initialize_velocities=False, but that alone is not a thermostat/barostat or biased-dynamics restart. equilibrate also writes checkpoints; its snapshot can be continued using restart_md with the saved ensemble/settings and a new trajectory destination.

If integration raises, output already flushed to the trajectory/log remains available. The most recent successfully written checkpoint is the restart point, which may be older than the last output frame. A failed snapshot write leaves the preceding snapshot intact. The API does not guarantee a new checkpoint at the exact failing step, and an abruptly terminated process may not update in-memory diagnostics.

docs.title: 5. Restart metadynamics with the correct history
docs.text:
Automatic biased restart supports input generated from MetadynamicsConfig fields, where neither plumed_file nor input_lines is supplied. The checkpoint bundles flushed HILLS and COLVAR history, the resolved PLUMED input, and cached bias results. Restoring from those snapshots does not depend on the original HILLS/COLVAR files still being present.

For example, after a generated metadynamics run:

from matmalib import mlmd

# Use the same AIMNet inference models and calculator settings as the first run.
simulation = mlmd(device="cpu")
simulation.restart_md(
    "biased_run/production.checkpoint.npz",
    steps=10000,
    trajectory="biased_run/production_part2.xyz",
    log_file="biased_run/production_part2.log",
)

The example assumes a previously created checkpoint; it is not an independent simulation. Restart creates biased_run/production_part2.plumed/ containing restored HILLS, COLVAR, and resolved plumed.dat. That directory must not already exist and its path must contain no whitespace. The step count and bias deposition schedule continue; growing histories are copied in chunks instead of loaded wholesale into memory. Small numerical differences from uninterrupted biased dynamics can arise from the finite precision of PLUMED history files.

Custom plumed_file or input_lines runs still write molecular checkpoints on the normal schedule, even when their input creates no HILLS or COLVAR. However, restart_md rejects their automatic continuation because arbitrary PLUMED actions may require additional external restart state. Restoring their molecular arrays alone would not reconstruct that bias. Use a workflow that explicitly handles all state required by the custom actions rather than treating such a checkpoint as an automatically portable biased restart.

Return to running simulations for ensemble selection, output diagnostics, and velocity initialization, or follow the metadynamics tutorial to create a generated bias configuration that supports this restart workflow.

docs.title: Build a periodic solvent box
docs.text:
mlmd.solvate places one solute, an optional single counterion, and an integer number of identical solvent molecules in an orthorhombic periodic cell. It chooses the solvent count from total mass divided by cell volume, then uses Packmol to avoid close intermolecular contacts. The result is a starting geometry for relaxation and equilibration, not an equilibrated liquid.

This tutorial starts with a reproducible packing plan, runs Packmol locally, and passes the resulting state to the simulation workflow. The browser examples inspect configuration and counting only. ASE and the Packmol executable run in your local Python environment.

docs.title: 1. Install the packing dependencies
docs.text:
From a checkout of matmalib, install the small solvation extra:

python -m pip install -e '.[solvation]'

This installs ASE and Packmol wheels. The package requires Packmol 21.2.1 or newer; the underlying periodic input format requires at least 20.15.0. If you installed Packmol separately, set packmol="/absolute/path/to/packmol". The default also checks for an executable alongside the active Python interpreter.

Solvation does not evaluate a potential, so it does not download AIMNet weights or require a GPU. Later AIMNet simulations need the MLMD dependencies described in the simulation tutorial.

docs.title: 2. Prepare and inspect a packing plan
docs.text:
Save this as prepare_box.py and run python prepare_box.py from a new working directory. It generates methane and water templates with ASE, then prepares a 15 Å box at a requested total density of 1.0 g/mL:

from ase.build import molecule
from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd()
solute = molecule("CH4")
solvent = molecule("H2O")

config = mlmd.SolvationConfig(
    cell=15.0,
    density_g_ml=1.0,
    tolerance=2.0,
    seed=12345,
    volume_samples=20000,
    work_dir="packing_plan",
    dry_run=True,
)
report = simulation.solvate(solute, solvent, config)

print("Status:", report.status)
for entry in report.molecules:
    print(entry["role"], entry["formula"], entry["count"])
print("Atoms:", report.atom_count)
print("Actual density:", report.achieved_density_g_ml, "g/mL")
print("Warnings:", report.warnings)
print("Packmol input:", report.files["packmol.inp"])

Expect one methane and 112 water molecules, or 341 atoms, using ASE's ordinary atomic masses. The achieved density is about 1.0006 g/mL. Rounding the solvent count explains the small difference from the target. A dry run returns Data, also available as simulation.data, with status "prepared"; there is no packed geometry yet. It requires work_dir, and you must omit output and output_format.

The directory contains normalized molecule templates, packmol.inp, and summary.json. Inspect the molecule counts, cell, tolerances, and warnings before packing. Dry runs work even when Packmol itself is unavailable, but still require ASE.

Inputs can instead be XYZ, extended XYZ, or PDB paths, matmalib State/Glycan objects, or ASE Atoms. Provide one molecule per component. A PDB must contain one model with no alternate conformations and full or blank occupancies; the reader does not infer missing atoms or add hydrogens. Template cell records are discarded because the new cell comes from SolvationConfig.cell.

docs.title: How the solvent count is chosen
docs.text:
The implementation calculates the target mass in atomic mass units, subtracts the solute and counterion masses, then rounds to the nearest positive integer number of solvent molecules:

V_mL = Lx * Ly * Lz * 1e-24
target_mass_u = density_g_ml * V_mL * N_A
N_solvent = floor((target_mass_u - fixed_mass_u) / solvent_mass_u + 0.5)
actual_density = (fixed_mass_u + N_solvent * solvent_mass_u) / (N_A * V_mL)

The volume is the whole cell, not a solvent-accessible volume obtained by subtracting the solute's van der Waals volume. Custom or isotope masses on input states/ASE atoms are retained and affect the count.

Change the box length or density in this browser exercise to see the integer jumps:

import math
from matmalib import mlmd

config = mlmd.SolvationConfig(cell=15.0, density_g_ml=1.0)
NA = 6.02214076e23
methane_mass, water_mass = 16.043, 18.015
volume_ml = config.cell ** 3 * 1e-24
count = math.floor(
    (config.density_g_ml * volume_ml * NA - methane_mass) / water_mass + 0.5
)
if count < 1:
    print("This example needs a larger box or greater target density.")
else:
    density = (methane_mass + count * water_mass) / (NA * volume_ml)
    print("Water molecules:", count)
    print("Total atoms:", 5 + 3 * count)
    print("Achieved density:", round(density, 6), "g/mL")

This cell illustrates the counting formula with stated masses; it does not run a packing calculation. The local API obtains masses from your actual inputs.

docs.title: 3. Run Packmol and keep the final state
docs.text:
Append this to prepare_box.py after inspecting the plan:

from dataclasses import replace

packed = simulation.solvate(
    solute,
    solvent,
    replace(config, dry_run=False, work_dir="packing_run"),
    output="solvated.xyz",
    output_format="state",
)
packing = simulation.data
print("Status:", packing.status)
print("Periodic axes:", packed.pbc)
print("Cell:", packed.cell)
print("Atoms:", len(packed.atoms))

The new work directory preserves the plan for comparison. output_format="state" writes extended XYZ and returns a State. Without output, the method also returns a State; with output="solvated.xyz" alone, it returns the output Path. The final state includes masses, charge, multiplicity, cell, full three-dimensional PBC, and solvation_report.

Packmol holds the solute's geometric center at the cell center and, when present, holds the counterion at a nearby nonoverlapping location. It translates and rotates solvent molecules while preserving each template's internal geometry. These are packing constraints only: they do not freeze the solute or counterion in subsequent dynamics. MD constraints belong in MinimizationConfig, EquilibrationConfig, or MDConfig.

After Packmol finishes, matmalib verifies atom order, count, elements, finite coordinates, bounds, fixed placements, and intermolecular distances including periodic images. A close contact triggers one retry with face padding of tolerance / 2; the initial files are retained with an initial_ prefix. A second failure raises and leaves a report/log for inspection. Packmol's own success message alone does not bypass these checks.

The generated packmol.inp can also be run manually from its directory using packmol < packmol.inp, as described in the Packmol user guide. That command produces the raw packed.pdb; use simulation.solvate for matmalib's final validation, metadata, and cell.xyz output.

docs.title: 4. Add a counterion and control electronic state
docs.text:
The current builder supports exactly one optional counterion molecule, which may contain one or several atoms. It does not infer charge balance, add multiple ions, choose a salt concentration, or support multiple solvent species.

from ase import Atoms
from matmalib import mlmd

# Replace these paths and charge with your prepared molecular inputs.
simulation = mlmd()
ion = Atoms("Cl", positions=[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]])
ion.info["charge"] = -1.0

plan = simulation.solvate(
    "cation.xyz", "water.xyz",
    mlmd.SolvationConfig(
        cell=(25.0, 25.0, 30.0),
        density_g_ml=1.0,
        counterion=ion,
        counterion_gap=0.5,
        charge=0.0,
        multiplicity=1,
        dry_run=True,
        work_dir="ionic_plan",
    ),
)
print(plan.fixed_centers_angstrom)
print(plan.molecules)

counterion_gap is the minimum requested surface-to-surface van der Waals gap between the solute and counterion, in Å. The placement must also satisfy the generic atomic tolerance, fit inside the cell, and avoid periodic overlaps. Neither input chemistry nor charge balance is inferred from a filename.

For completed packing, charge=None sums component charge metadata: one solute, one counterion if present, and N_solvent solvent charges. An explicit charge overrides that sum. Set the combined system's multiplicity directly; molecular multiplicities are not additive. Ordinary XYZ files frequently lack this metadata, so supply explicit values when needed.

docs.title: 5. Choose controls and interpret diagnostics
docs.text:
Control Default Effect cell 30.0 Å One cubic length or (Lx, Ly, Lz); no triclinic packing. Lengths are rounded to 0.001 Å for PDB consistency. density_g_ml 1.0 Total target density; must leave enough target mass for at least one solvent molecule. tolerance 2.0 Å Minimum intermolecular atom-center separation used by packing and collision checks; not a van der Waals radius. counterion_gap 0.5 Å Additional solute/counterion surface gap. nloop / timeout 1000 / 600 s Packmol optimization loops and subprocess time limit. seed 12345 Positive integer used for packing and volume sampling, at most 2147483647. volume_samples 200000 Samples per template for the diagnostic sphere-union volume estimate; at least 2. vdw_radii {} Element-to-radius overrides in Å; otherwise use ASE's van der Waals radii. work_dir None Preserve inputs, logs, cells, and JSON here; otherwise use temporary storage. Required for a dry run. overwrite False Protect output and previously generated work-directory files.

Each molecule's volume is estimated as the union of its atomic van der Waals spheres, including overlaps; single-atom volumes are analytic. vdw_volume_standard_error_angstrom3 measures Monte Carlo sampling error, not uncertainty in the radii or a liquid's thermodynamic volume. Increasing volume_samples refines this diagnostic; it does not change the mass-based solvent count.

estimated_vdw_packing_fraction is the sum of those molecular volumes divided by cell volume. A value above one adds a warning that packing may be difficult. It is not a measured occupied fraction of the final periodic configuration. The chosen radii also affect whether the centered solute and counterion fit, so missing radii must be supplied, for example vdw_radii={"Cl": 1.8}.

PDB intermediates limit the box to 99,999 atoms and cell lengths to the range that rounds to 0.001–9999.999 Å. Reusing a work directory requires overwrite=True; only known generated files are replaced, and unrelated files are preserved. Avoid using input templates at the generated solute.pdb, solvent.pdb, or counterion.pdb paths in that directory.

docs.title: Outputs to retain
docs.text:
File or object Purpose summary.json, simulation.data.summary Counts, masses, target/achieved density, cell, volume estimates, warnings, status, and failure details. solute.pdb, solvent.pdb, optional counterion.pdb Centered templates used for packing. packmol.inp, packmol.log, packed.pdb Reproducible input, subprocess output, and raw packing result. cell.xyz Final extended XYZ with periodic cell, masses, and electronic-state metadata. cell.pdb Final geometry/cell for inspection; prefer extended XYZ to preserve simulation metadata. State.solvation_report Packing report attached to the returned state.

Save packing = simulation.data before the next operation: the interface replaces .data each time. If packing raises, inspect .data.status, .data.error, and the preserved work-directory log. Increase the cell or reduce target density when the fixed molecule cannot fit or the requested packing is too dense; increasing iteration limits does not make an impossible geometry feasible.

docs.title: 6. Relax and equilibrate the cell
docs.text:
With the MLMD environment installed, continue from the completed packed state:

from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd()  # AIMNet defaults; resolves model weights when first used
relaxed = simulation.minimize("solvated.xyz", mlmd.MinimizationConfig())
ready = simulation.equilibrate(
    relaxed,
    mlmd.EquilibrationConfig(
        steps=2000,
        timestep_fs=0.5,
        ensemble="NPT",
        pressure_bar=1.0,
        temperature_K=300.0,
        log_file="box_equilibration.log",
    ),
    output="equilibrated.xyz",
    output_format="state",
)
print(simulation.data.summary)

This is a workflow example, not a convergence criterion. Evaluate whether the potential describes your solute, solvent, ions, and thermodynamic conditions; monitor density, temperature, forces, and structural relaxation. NPT needs a stress-capable calculator and does not support fixed atoms, SHAKE, or persistent center-of-mass constraints. NVT Langevin dynamics supports those constraints when appropriate. Continue with production MD or metadynamics after assessing equilibration.

docs.title: Run molecular dynamics with mlmd
docs.text:
mlmd takes a geometry, attaches a potential, and performs minimization, equilibration, and production dynamics through ASE. Its default potential averages four AIMNet2-2025 B97-3c/D3 models. You can also supply an ASE calculator for another potential. Trajectories stream to disk; the interface retains diagnostics and the current geometry rather than every frame.

This tutorial first runs a small CPU example with ASE's EMT calculator to teach the workflow without downloading models. It then runs a molecular example with AIMNet. The Run buttons inspect real configuration objects in the browser; simulations themselves run in local Python with the optional dependencies installed.

docs.title: 1. Install the simulation support
docs.text:
Use the current source checkout for these newly added APIs; the previously published PyPI release may not include them. Cloning the source repository requires GitHub access to it. From the repository directory in your Python environment, choose one installation:

# A small environment for the EMT examples and other supplied ASE calculators:
python -m pip install -e '.[md]'

# Or add AIMNet and PyTorch for machine-learning potentials:
python -m pip install -e '.[aimnet]'

# Or install all simulation extras, including solvation and PLUMED bindings:
python -m pip install -e '.[mlmd]'

The package requires Python 3.12 or newer; the repository's complete environment selects Python 3.12. With Conda, the complete environment also supplies the native PLUMED kernel and command-line tools:

conda env update -n matmalib -f environment.yml
conda activate matmalib
python -m pip check
python -c "from matmalib import mlmd; import ase; print(ase.__version__)"

md installs ASE; aimnet adds AIMNet and PyTorch. solvation adds ASE and Packmol, and metadynamics adds ASE and the PLUMED Python bindings. Those bindings alone do not supply the native PLUMED installation. Choose a PyTorch build appropriate for your CPU/GPU environment. Importing mlmd and creating its configurations do not load models or import these optional simulation packages.

docs.title: 2. Inspect a run before executing it
docs.text:
Configurations are dataclasses nested under mlmd. They hold parameters; validation that depends on the system or operation happens when you call minimize, equilibrate, or run_md. Constructing a config is not a simulation or a complete validity check.

from dataclasses import asdict, replace
from matmalib import mlmd

config = mlmd.MDConfig(
    steps=2000,
    timestep_fs=0.5,
    ensemble="NVT",
    temperature_K=300.0,
    seed=17,
    trajectory_interval=20,
)
print("Production duration (ps):", config.steps * config.timestep_fs / 1000)
print("Regular frame spacing (fs):", config.trajectory_interval * config.timestep_fs)
print("Thermostat:", asdict(config)["thermostat"])
short = replace(config, steps=100)
print("Original steps:", config.steps, "Short run steps:", short.steps)

This plans 1 ps of dynamics with regular saved frames 10 fs apart. The initial and final frames are also saved, so the final interval can be shorter than the requested spacing. Increasing trajectory_interval reduces disk output, not the number of force evaluations.

docs.title: 3. Run a complete CPU example
docs.text:
Save the following as run_emt.py in a working directory, then run python run_emt.py. It creates a small periodic copper system and performs a short minimization, NVT equilibration, and NVE production run. EMT demonstrates the API and integrators; it is not an ML potential and this copper example should not be reused with the default AIMNet models.

from pathlib import Path
from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

run = Path("emt_run")
run.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())
initial = bulk("Cu", cubic=True)  # four atoms, cell and PBC included
initial.positions[0, 0] += 0.03

relaxed = simulation.minimize(
    initial,
    mlmd.MinimizationConfig(
        optimizer="FIRE", fmax=0.02, steps=200,
        trajectory=run / "minimization.xyz",
        log_file=run / "minimization.log",
    ),
    output=run / "relaxed.xyz", output_format="state",
)
optimization = simulation.data

ready = simulation.equilibrate(
    relaxed,
    mlmd.EquilibrationConfig(
        steps=20, timestep_fs=0.2, temperature_K=100,
        seed=17, log_interval=5,
        trajectory=run / "equilibration.xyz",
        log_file=run / "equilibration.log",
    ),
    output=run / "equilibrated.xyz", output_format="state",
)
equilibration = simulation.data

trajectory = simulation.run_md(
    ready,
    mlmd.MDConfig(
        steps=40, timestep_fs=0.2, ensemble="NVE",
        initialize_velocities=False,
        trajectory=run / "production.xyz", trajectory_interval=10,
        log_file=run / "production.log", log_interval=10,
    ),
)
production = simulation.data
print("Minimization converged:", optimization.converged)
print("Equilibration steps:", equilibration.steps)
print("Production:", production.status, production.steps, "steps")
print("Production duration (fs):", production.simulation_time_fs)
print("Trajectory:", trajectory)
print("Checkpoint:", production.checkpoint_file)
print("Mean temperature (K):", production.averages["temperature_K"])

Expect a converged minimization, 20 equilibration steps, and a complete 40-step production run lasting 8 fs. production.xyz has five frames at steps 0, 10, 20, 30, and 40. Each phase has its own output files; production starts its own step/time count at zero. This very short run checks the workflow, not thermodynamic equilibration or sampling convergence.

The equilibration result carries masses and momenta into production. initialize_velocities=False explicitly requires them. The production temperature_K setting does not thermostat NVE or rescale existing velocities. To repeat the example, use a new output directory, remove its earlier outputs yourself, or deliberately set overwrite=True in each configuration whose files you want to replace. Existing outputs are protected by default.

docs.title: Check the energy trace
docs.text:
Run this after the example, from the same directory:

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

records = np.loadtxt(Path("emt_run") / "production.log", ndmin=2)
time_fs = records[:, 1]
total_energy_eV = records[:, 8]
print("Total-energy range (eV):", np.ptp(total_energy_eV))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(time_fs, total_energy_eV - total_energy_eV[0], marker="o")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (fs)", ylabel="Total-energy change (eV)")
fig.savefig("emt_run/energy_change.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

The log's header identifies its columns. Assess an NVE timestep using energy behavior over a suitably long test and compare smaller timesteps. Temperature fluctuations in a four-atom example are not representative of a bulk sample. ASE explains how timestep choice affects numerical stability in its MD guide.

docs.title: 4. Use the default AIMNet ensemble
docs.text:
With the aimnet extra installed, save this separate example as run_aimnet.py. It creates an isolated neutral water molecule and uses the actual default ML potential. The first energy/force evaluation can download the model weights and take longer than subsequent steps.

from pathlib import Path
from ase.build import molecule
from matmalib import mlmd

run = Path("aimnet_water_run")
run.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
simulation = mlmd(device="cpu")  # use "cuda" with a suitable GPU installation
trajectory = simulation.run_md(
    molecule("H2O"),
    mlmd.MDConfig(
        charge=0, multiplicity=1,
        steps=200, timestep_fs=0.25, temperature_K=300,
        ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin", seed=23,
        minimization=mlmd.MinimizationConfig(fmax=0.03, steps=1000),
        equilibration=mlmd.EquilibrationConfig(
            steps=100, timestep_fs=0.25, temperature_K=300, seed=23,
            log_file=run / "equilibration.log",
        ),
        trajectory=run / "production.xyz",
        log_file=run / "production.log",
        trajectory_interval=10, log_interval=10,
    ),
)
report = simulation.data
print("Trajectory:", trajectory)
print("Models:", report.models)
print("Preparation phases:", list(report.phases))
print("Final temperature (K):", report.final["temperature_K"])
print("Mean ensemble energy spread (eV):", report.averages["energy_std_eV"])

This requests 25 fs of equilibration and 50 fs of production. The numbers make a small initial run, not a recommended research sampling duration. Use your own XYZ/PDB path or State in place of molecule("H2O") after choosing a suitable model, charge, multiplicity, cell, and simulation protocol.

The default AIMNet2-2025 family covers H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, As, Se, Br, and I. Its training domain is molecular systems; a periodic cell does not make it a potential for metallic copper or arbitrary bulk materials. Open-shell systems need a model designed for their spin treatment. Review the AIMNet model selection guide for your chemistry before running it.

docs.title: Select or supply a potential
docs.text:
Construction Model selection mlmd() All four aimnet2-b973c-2025-d3_0 through _3 members; energy, forces, and requested stress are averaged. mlmd(model_path="aimnet2-2025") The same four-member family. mlmd(model_path="aimnet2-b973c-2025-d3_0") One registry member. Ensemble disagreement is unavailable for a single member. mlmd(model_path="/models/inference.pt") One existing AIMNet inference file. mlmd(model_path=["/models/a.pt", "/models/b.pt"]) The mean of the supplied inference models. mlmd(calculator=calculator) Use the supplied ASE calculator instance; do not also set model_path.

For the default models, the resolver first checks the working directory and its checkpoints/ subdirectory for matching files, including aimnet2_2025_b973c_d3_0.pt through _3.pt. Otherwise AIMNet handles registry downloads. A missing explicit file path raises an error; it does not silently choose a different potential. Supply inference files rather than raw training checkpoints. Other supported family aliases include aimnet2, aimnet2-b973c, aimnet2-nse, aimnet2-pd, and aimnet2-rxn; matmalib family aliases expand to four members.

device and compile_model are explicit constructor arguments. Additional AIMNet calculator options go in model_kwargs. compile_model=True raises when TORCH_COMPILE_DISABLE=1 or TORCH_DISABLE_NATIVE_JIT=1 conflicts with that request; the library does not change those environment variables. An injected calculator must provide energy and forces, and stress for NPT. The interface clears input calculator attachments and uses the calculator you supplied to mlmd.

docs.title: 5. Choose the ensemble and coupling
docs.text:
Configuration Integrator Requirements and interpretation ensemble="NVE" ASE velocity Verlet No thermostat or barostat. Temperature is only an initialization parameter when drawing velocities. ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin" Langevin Default NVT choice. Friction is the reciprocal of thermostat_time_fs; accepts the supported constraints. ensemble="NVT", thermostat="berendsen" NVT Berendsen Temperature coupling uses thermostat_time_fs. ensemble="NVT", thermostat="nose-hoover" Nosé–Hoover chains Uses thermostat_time_fs and thermostat_chain; constraints are rejected. ensemble="NPT", barostat="mtk" Isotropic MTK with chains Default NPT choice. Full 3D PBC, a finite-volume cell, stress, and no constraints required. ensemble="NPT", barostat="berendsen" NPT Berendsen Same geometry/constraint requirements; additionally uses compressibility_per_bar.

NPT integrators include their thermostat; the NVT thermostat selector does not choose a separate NPT thermostat. pressure_bar defaults to 1 bar, thermostat_time_fs to 100 fs, and barostat_time_fs to 1000 fs in MDConfig. Chain lengths default to three. EquilibrationConfig instead defaults to a 10 fs thermostat time. Berendsen coupling suppresses equilibrium fluctuations, so its output should not be treated as exact canonical or isothermal-isobaric sampling. See ASE's ensemble documentation.

Here is an independent short NPT mechanics example using EMT and a periodic copper cell:

from ase.build import bulk
from ase.calculators.emt import EMT
from matmalib import mlmd

simulation = mlmd(calculator=EMT())
trajectory = simulation.run_md(
    bulk("Cu", cubic=True),
    mlmd.MDConfig(
        ensemble="NPT", barostat="mtk", pressure_bar=1.0,
        steps=20, timestep_fs=0.2, temperature_K=100, seed=31,
        thermostat_time_fs=100, barostat_time_fs=1000,
        trajectory="npt_run/trajectory.xyz", log_file="npt_run/md.log",
    ),
)
print("Final volume (angstrom^3):", simulation.data.final["volume_A3"])

For Berendsen NPT, supply a compressibility appropriate to your system. Its default 4.57e-5 per bar is a water-like value, not a universal material constant. Geometry minimization optimizes atomic positions at the supplied cell; it is not a cell relaxation. A common liquid workflow is minimization, NPT equilibration to adjust volume, then production in the desired ensemble. A combined run preserves the cell produced by NPT equilibration.

docs.title: 6. Control geometry, velocities, and constraints
docs.text:
Inputs may be a .xyz/.extxyz/.pdb/.ent path, a matmalib State (including Glycan), or ASE Atoms. A multi-frame path is read sequentially and its last frame is used. Input objects are copied. Config values for cell, pbc, charge, and multiplicity override input metadata; otherwise input values are preserved, with charge 0 and multiplicity 1 as fallbacks. Plain XYZ files do not supply a periodic cell.

Coordinates are in angstrom, energies in eV, forces in eV/angstrom, time in fs, temperature in K, and pressure in bar. State.velocities uses angstrom/fs, while State.momenta uses ASE's native momentum units. If a state has both arrays, momenta take precedence when reading it. Returned states preserve cell, PBC, charge, multiplicity, masses, and supported constraints.

from dataclasses import asdict
from matmalib import mlmd

config = mlmd.MDConfig(
    ensemble="NVT", thermostat="langevin",
    fixed_atoms=(0,),          # zero-based atom positions
    fix_com=True,
    initialize_velocities=None,
    max_velocity_angstrom_fs=0.1,
)
for key in ("ensemble", "thermostat", "fixed_atoms", "fix_com",
            "initialize_velocities", "max_velocity_angstrom_fs"):
    print(key, "=", asdict(config)[key])

The snippet inspects settings; whether atom 0 exists and leaves enough free degrees of freedom is checked against the real system when running.

Setting Behavior initialize_velocities=None Preserve existing momenta; otherwise draw velocities at temperature_K using the seeded NumPy generator. initialize_velocities=True Draw new velocities, even if the input has momenta. initialize_velocities=False Require input momenta/velocities; missing values raise. remove_com_motion=True Remove center-of-mass motion only when initializing an unconstrained system with more than one atom. It does not constrain later dynamics. fix_com=True Add a persistent ASE center-of-mass constraint. fixed_atoms=(0, 2) Fix selected zero-based atom positions; existing fixed-atom constraints are retained. shake_hydrogens=True Add fixed-length constraints to nearby pairs involving H, using shake_cutoff=1.3 angstrom and shake_tolerance=1e-6; also add persistent center-of-mass fixation. hydrogen_mass=... Replace all hydrogen masses with the given amu value. heavy_mass_multiplier=... Multiply non-hydrogen masses by this positive factor.

SHAKE pair selection uses the distance cutoff, not a chemical bond-order model. Inspect the geometry and choose the cutoff deliberately. NPT and NVT Nosé–Hoover reject all constraints, including inherited constraints and fix_com. Langevin and NVE support the documented fixed atoms/SHAKE workflow. A system with no remaining free degrees of freedom is rejected.

Mass modification is scaling, not mass-conserving hydrogen mass repartitioning. Existing velocities are preserved when masses change, so kinetic energies and momenta change accordingly. This alters the dynamics; validate your timestep and interpretation. A combined equilibration/production call applies mass settings once and carries velocities into production. If you run phases as separate method calls, avoid requesting the same heavy-atom multiplication again on an already scaled state.

docs.title: 7. Minimize and combine preparation phases
docs.text:
MinimizationConfig defaults to FIRE, fmax=0.05 eV/angstrom, at most 10,000 steps, and maxstep=0.1 angstrom. Optimizer names are matched case-insensitively to ASE's exported optimizer classes, for example BFGS, LBFGS, and BFGSLineSearch. Additional settings go in optimizer_kwargs; use the dedicated fields for maxstep, trajectory, and log paths. maxstep is passed when the chosen optimizer accepts it explicitly. FIRE enables its downhill check by default.

require_convergence=True raises if minimization ends above the requested force threshold. The failed optimization report remains in simulation.data, including converged, initial_fmax, final_fmax, and target_fmax. With require_convergence=False, the final unconverged state is returned; check its report before using it. Minimization preserves explicitly supplied momenta, so request initialize_velocities=True afterward if you intend a fresh thermal initialization.

MDConfig(minimization=..., equilibration=...), as used in the AIMNet example, runs preparation in order. Each phase must use distinct output paths. The production report keeps preparation summaries in phases, and adds total_simulation_time_fs, total_elapsed_seconds, and pooled workflow_averages/workflow_finite_samples. Individual production statistics remain under summary, averages, initial, and final. Ordinary equilibration is unbiased unless its own mode and metadynamics configuration request bias.

An EquilibrationConfig supports the MD settings and an optional minimization, but cannot contain another equilibration. It defaults to 2,000 NVT steps, no trajectory, equilibration.log, and no finite-force threshold. Both standalone equilibration and production write checkpoints even when no PLUMED calculation is involved.

docs.title: 8. Read output and diagnose a run
docs.text:
minimize and equilibrate return a State by default.
